correctness.rationale: Walsh inversion leaves only the empty and full character because each proper marginal is uniform. Pointwise nonnegativity gives |theta|<=1 and the inversion also proves the converse. The first-moment difference is theta times the full-character coefficient of the absolute sign sum. Global sign reversal makes that coefficient zero in odd dimension. In even dimension a sign sum multiplied by n-2 equals the sum of its n single-flip neighbors. The triangle inequality (also for complex coefficients) and the bijective flips between the parity classes give (n-2)E+<=nE- and (n-2)E-<=nE+, where E± are normalized class means. Their sum is positive for a nonzero coefficient vector because otherwise the sign sum vanishes identically, which forces every coefficient to vanish. Rearrangement gives |E+-E-|/(E++E-)<=1/(n-1). For the all-ones vector in even dimension, the parity class not containing balanced signs has |S|>=2 throughout, so all single-flip sums have the same weak sign and the triangle inequality is exact on that class. One coefficient sign change exchanges the means and realizes the other ratio endpoint. The n=2 two-value formula attains 0 at the degenerate lower endpoint and gives the same sharp comparison; for n>=4 the lower bound is positive. The all-dimension argument was checked directly against RESULT.md, Proof; the sign enumeration was inspected, not executed, and is supplementary.

value.rationale: The theorem quantifies the worst loss from using a prescribed half of the sign cube rather than all sign patterns for all first moments of linear forms. It gives exact preservation in odd dimension and an attained, dimension-dependent error in even dimension, including the two-dimensional degeneracy. The parity-class averaging explains the sharp uniform control rather than merely evaluating a flat witness.
